[Part 2]
You will hear a city council officer giving a talk about a new bike-sharing scheme. First you have time to look at questions 11 to 20. The bike-sharing scheme will launch in the month of June. The initial fleet will consist of 250 bicycles. Users can unlock a bike using a smartphone application. The maximum allowed rental duration per ride is three hours. Helmets can be borrowed free of charge from the central hub. Maintenance work on all bikes is performed every two weeks. The council officer emphasized that the scheme was designed mainly to reduce traffic congestion across the downtown area. Installation costs for docking stations were funded by a grant from the national transport ministry.

[Part 3]
You will hear two university students, Liam and Sophia, discussing their recent archaeology fieldwork project. First you have time to look at questions 21 to 30. The excavation site was first discovered in the year 2018. The team recovered a total of 140 pottery sherds. The oldest layer of sediment dated back to the twelfth century. Fieldwork logs were submitted to the university database every evening. The students spent 15 days working at the excavation site. Sophia will present their preliminary findings at a conference in October. Liam admitted he was surprised to find the site heavily overgrown with vegetation when they first arrived. Sophia noted that accurately recording artifact depth proved to be the most challenging aspect of the work. The supervisor recommended that their final report concentrate on analyzing trade network evidence found at the site. Liam and Sophia agreed that future teams should carry out a drone aerial mapping survey before digging further.

[Part 4]
You will hear part of a lecture on the history of cartography and mapmaking. First you have time to look at questions 31 to 40. The earliest surviving clay map fragments were created in ancient Mesopotamia. Early Greek cartographers were among the first to calculate Earth's circumference. Ptolemy introduced a systematic grid based on latitude and longitude. During the Middle Ages, European maps often placed east at the top. The Mercator projection was originally created to assist with sea navigation. Portolan charts were noted for their highly accurate coastal outlines. The invention of the printing press led to a rapid drop in map prices. In the nineteenth century, thematic maps began illustrating data on disease. Aerial photography transformed cartography during the First World War. Modern satellite mapping enables real-time tracking of environmental change.

passages.title: The Growth of Vertical Farming
passages.text: Vertical farming involves cultivating plants in stacked layers within controlled indoor environments. Proponents argue it offers a sustainable solution to food security in growing urban populations. Vertical farming facilities often operate inside repurposed urban warehouses. Controlled indoor agriculture uses up to 95 percent less water than traditional farming. Artificial LED lighting allows crops to grow for 24 hours a day. Hydroponic systems deliver nutrients directly to plant roots. Leafy greens and herbs currently account for the majority of commercial crops. The initial capital cost of equipping a vertical farm remains high due to expensive technology. A major environmental benefit cited by researchers is eliminating agricultural runoff, which severely pollutes freshwater ecosystems in open-field farming. Critics emphasize that high energy demands are primarily driven by continuous climate control and artificial lighting systems inside the facility. The passage discusses global developments in indoor farming without specifying where the first commercial facility opened. Because indoor environments are completely sealed against pests, vertical farms do not require chemical pesticide applications. Grain crops such as wheat and rice are not grown profitably indoors because their low market value cannot offset high electricity costs. Automated robotic sensors are increasingly deployed to monitor plant health and growth rates across vertical stacks. Advancements in energy-efficient LED lights have actually reduced electricity costs for vertical farm operators over the past decade.

passages.title: How Bilingualism Shapes the Brain
passages.text: For decades, researchers believed learning two languages simultaneously might confuse young children. Modern neuroscience has overturned this view, revealing significant cognitive advantages. Brain imaging studies show that bilingual individuals possess greater gray matter density. Bilingual children demonstrate superior performance in tests of executive function. Managing two languages requires constant mental switching and attentional control. Lifelong bilingualism has been shown to delay symptoms of dementia by roughly four years. Researchers test cognitive control using tasks that involve conflicting visual cues. Educational programs that immerse students in a second language are growing in popularity. Studies indicate that the bilingual advantage is most evident when individuals must ignore irrelevant distractions and focus on task-relevant information. Neuroscience research proves that both languages in a bilingual brain remain permanently active at the same time, forcing the brain to suppress one language while speaking the other. Early mid-century studies claiming negative effects were flawed because researchers failed to control for socioeconomic factors among participants. Cognitive flexibility gained from managing two languages enables bilingual adults to acquire third languages faster than monolinguals. Studies show that bilingual children reach key speech milestones, such as producing their first words, at the same age as monolinguals, not much later. The passage mentions specific areas like the prefrontal cortex but does not state whether all brain regions benefit equally. Comparative testing reveals that elderly bilinguals retain stronger working memory skills compared to monolingual peers.

passages.title: Life at Deep-Sea Hydrothermal Vents
passages.text: Discovered in 1977 near the Galápagos Rift, deep-sea hydrothermal vents revolutionized marine biology by demonstrating that complex ecosystems can thrive in total darkness without sunlight. Hydrothermal vents form along oceanic ridges where tectonic plates pull apart. Water emerging from vents can reach temperatures exceeding 400 degrees Celsius. Extreme pressure prevents superheated vent water from boiling into steam. Chemosynthetic bacteria form the foundation of the vent ecosystem's food web. Giant tube worms living near vents can grow up to two metres long. Mineral deposits around vents contain high concentrations of copper and zinc. The discovery surprised marine biologists primarily because life was previously thought impossible without solar energy driving photosynthesis. Instead of sunlight, chemosynthetic bacteria generate organic matter by oxidizing chemical compounds such as hydrogen sulfide emitted from vent fluids. Giant tube worms lack a mouth and digestive tract, relying entirely on billions of symbiotic bacteria residing inside specialized internal tissues. Mining conglomerates are surveying deep-sea hydrothermal vents because volcanic fluids deposit rich concentrations of valuable seafloor metals. Located thousands of metres below the surface, vent ecosystems are insulated from surface atmospheric climate changes. Geological shifts frequently clog vent conduits, causing individual hydrothermal chimneys to shut down within a few decades. Attempts to keep giant tube worms alive in laboratories have failed due to the difficulty of replicating deep-sea pressure. Astrobiologists hypothesize that hydrothermal vents similar to Earth's may exist beneath ice crusts on moons like Europa and Enceladus.

questions.prompt: Some people believe that governments should subsidize healthy food options such as fresh fruit and vegetables, while others argue that public funds should be spent on healthcare infrastructure. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
questions.modelAnswer: Subsidizing nutritious foods versus allocating public revenues to healthcare infrastructure represents a key debate in public health policy. While upgrading medical facilities provides essential emergency care, I believe subsidizing healthy food yields far greater long-term preventative health benefits for society. On the one hand, advocates of expanding healthcare infrastructure emphasize the immediate necessity of modern medical care. Advanced hospitals, state-of-the-art diagnostic machinery, and well-equipped emergency rooms are essential for treating acute illnesses, injuries, and complex diseases. Without sufficient funding for hospital beds and medical staff, healthcare systems risk collapse during health crises. Furthermore, infrastructure investments ensure that specialized treatments remain accessible to all citizens regardless of income. On the other hand, proponents of food subsidies argue that prevention is more effective than cure. Dietary habits strongly influence the prevalence of chronic conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular diseases. In many countries, fresh fruits and vegetables are more expensive than processed, calorie-dense foods, forcing low-income families toward unhealthy choices. Subsidizing organic produce lowers financial barriers, encouraging healthier eating habits and dramatically reducing the incidence of lifestyle-related illnesses. In my view, prioritizing food subsidies is a more sustainable approach. By reducing dietary health risks across the population, governments can prevent chronic conditions before they require costly hospital treatment, ultimately easing the burden on healthcare infrastructure.
